{{Short description|Triangle with specific characteristics}}
A '''Brahmagupta triangle''' is a [[triangle]] whose side lengths are consecutive positive integers and area is a positive integer.<ref name="Surya">{{cite journal |last1=R. A. Beauregard and E. R. Suryanarayan |title=The Brahmagupta Triangles |journal=The College Mathematics Journal |date=January 1998 |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=13–17 |doi=10.1080/07468342.1998.11973907 |url=https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/mathdl/CMJ/methodoflastresort.pdf |access-date=6 June 2024}}</ref><ref name="Herb">{{cite journal |last1=Herb Bailey and William Gosnell |title=Heronian Triangles with Sides in Arithmetic Progression: An Inradius Perspective |journal=Mathematics Magazine |date=October 2012 |volume=85 |issue=4 |pages=290–294 |doi=10.4169/math.mag.85.4.290}}</ref> The triangle whose side lengths are 3, 4, 5 is a Brahmagupta triangle and so also is the triangle whose side lengths are 13, 14, 15. The Brahmagupta triangle is a special case of the [[Heronian triangle]] which is a triangle whose side lengths and area are all positive integers but the side lengths need not necessarily be consecutive integers. A Brahmagupta triangle is called as such in honor of the Indian astronomer and mathematician [[Brahmagupta]]  (c. 598 – c. 668 CE) who gave a list of the first eight such triangles without explaining the method by which he computed that list.<ref name=Surya/><ref>{{cite book |last= Venkatachaliyengar |first= K.  |date=1988 |editor-last= Subbarayappa |editor-first=B. V.  |title=Scientific Heritage of India: Proceedings of a National Seminar, September 19-21, 1986, Bangalore |publisher= The Mythic Society, Bangalore |pages=36–48 |chapter=The Development of Mathematics in Ancient India: The Role of Brahmagupta |isbn=}}</ref>

A Brahmagupta triangle is also called a '''Fleenor-Heronian triangle''' in honor of Charles R. Fleenor who discussed the concept in a paper published in 1996.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Charles R. Fleenor |title=Heronian Triangles with Consecutive Integer Sides |journal=Journal of Recreational Mathematics |date=1996 |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=113–115}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=N. J. A. Sloane |title=A003500 |url=https://oeis.org/A003500 |website=Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences |publisher=The OEIS Foundation Inc. |access-date=6 June 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Definition:Fleenor-Heronian Triangle |url=https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Definition:Fleenor-Heronian_Triangle |website=Proof-Wiki |access-date=6 June 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vo Dong To |title=Finding all Fleenor-Heronian triangles |journal=Journal of Recreational Mathematics |date=2003 |volume=32 |issue=4 |pages=298–301}}</ref> Some of the other names by which Brahmagupta triangles are known are '''super-Heronian triangle'''<ref>{{cite web |last1=William H. Richardson |title=Super-Heronian Triangles |url=https://www.math.wichita.edu/~richardson/heronian/heronian.html |website=www.wichita.edu |publisher=Wichita State University |access-date=7 June 2024}}</ref> and '''almost-equilateral Heronian triangle'''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roger B Nelsen |title=Almost Equilateral Heronian Triangles |journal=Mathematics Magazine |date=2020 |volume=93 |issue=5 |pages=378–379|doi=10.1080/0025570X.2020.1817708 }}</ref>

The problem of finding all Brahmagupta triangles is an old problem. A closed form solution of the problem was found by [[Reinhold Hoppe]] in 1880.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=H. W. Gould |title=A triangle with integral sides and area |journal=Fibonacci Quarterly |date=1973 |volume=11 |pages=27–39 |doi=10.1080/00150517.1973.12430863 |url=https://www.fq.math.ca/Scanned/11-1/gould.pdf |access-date=7 June 2024}}</ref>

==Generating Brahmagupta triangles==

Let the side lengths of a Brahmagupta triangle be {{math|''t'' &minus; 1}}, {{mvar|t}}, and {{math|''t'' + 1}}, where {{mvar|t}} is an integer greater than 1. Using [[Heron's formula]], the area {{mvar|A}} of the triangle can be shown to be
<math display=block >A = \frac{t}{2} \sqrt{3 \left( \left(\tfrac{t}{2}\right)^2 -1 \right)  } </math>
Since {{mvar|A}} has to be an integer, {{mvar|t}} must be even and so it can be taken as <math>t=2x </math> where {{mvar|x}} is an integer. Thus, 
<math display=block >A = x\sqrt{3(x^2-1) } </math>
Since <math display=inline> \sqrt{3(x^2-1) } </math> has to be an integer, one must have <math>x^2-1 =3y^2  </math> for some integer  {{mvar|y}}. Hence,  {{mvar|x}} must satisfy the following [[Diophantine equation]]:
<math display=block >x^2 - 3y^2 = 1 .</math>
This is an example of the so-called [[Pell's equation]] {{math|1=''x''{{sup|2}} &minus; ''Ny''{{sup|2}} = 1}} with {{math|1=''N'' = 3}}. The methods for solving the Pell's equation can be applied to find values of the integers {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}}.

[[File:BrahmaguptaTriangle.png|thumb|A Brahmagupta triangle where {{mvar|x{{sub|n}}}} and {{mvar|y{{sub|n}}}} are integers satisfying the equation <math> x_n^2-3y_n^2=1</math>.]]

Obviously {{math|1=''x'' = 2}}, {{math|1=''y'' = 1}} is a solution of the equation {{math|1=''x''{{sup|2}} &minus; 3''y''{{sup|2}} = 1}}. Taking this as an initial solution {{math|1=''x''{{sub|1}} = 2}}, {{math|1=''y''{{sub|1}} = 1}}, the set of all solutions {{math|{{mset|(''{{mvar|x{{sub|n}}}}'', ''{{mvar|y{{sub|n}}}}'')}}}} of the equation can be generated using the following recurrence relations<ref name=Surya/>
<math display=block >\begin{align}
  & x_{n+1} = 2x_n + 3y_n, && y_{n+1} = x_n + 2y_n, && n = 1,2,\ldots \\[2pt]
  & \quad x_1 = 2. && \quad y_1 = 1.
\end{align}</math>
or by the following relations with additional initial solutions {{math|1=''x''{{sub|2}} = 7}}, {{math|1=''y''{{sub|2}} = 4}}:
<math display=block >\begin{align}
  & x_{n+1} = 4x_n - x_{n-1}, && y_{n+1} = 4y_n - y_{n-1}, && n = 2,3,\ldots \\[2pt]
  & \quad x_1 = 2,\ x_2 = 7. && \quad y_1 = 1,\ y_2 = 4.
\end{align}</math>

They can also be generated using the following property:
<math display=block >
x_n+\sqrt{3} y_n = \left(x_1 + \sqrt{3}y_1 \right)^n, \quad n=1,2, \ldots
</math>
The following are the first eight values of {{mvar|x{{sub|n}}}} and {{mvar|y{{sub|n}}}} and the corresponding Brahmagupta triangles:
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! {{mvar|n}} !! 1 !! 2 !! 3 !! 4 !! 5 !! 6 !! 7 !! 8 
|-
| {{mvar|x{{sub|n}}}} || 2 || 7 || 26 || 97 || 362 || 1351 || 5042 || 18817  
|-
| {{mvar|y{{sub|n}}}} || 1 || 4 || 15 || 56 || 209 || 780 || 2911 || 10864
|-
|Brahmagupta<br />triangle||3,4,5||13,14,15||51,52,53||193,194,195||723,724,725||2701,2702,2703||10083,10084,10085||37633,37634,37635 
|}
The sequence {{math|{{mset|''x{{sub|n}}''}}}} is entry {{OEIS link|A001075}} in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences ([[OEIS]]) and the sequence {{math|{{mset|''y{{sub|n}}''}}}} is entry {{OEIS link|A001353}} in OEIS.

==Generalized Brahmagupta triangles==
In a  Brahmagupta triangle the side lengths form an integer [[arithmetic progression]] with a common difference 1. A generalized Brahmagupta triangle is a Heronian triangle in which the side lengths form an arithmetic progression of positive integers. Generalized Brahmagupta triangles can be easily constructed from Brahmagupta triangles. If <math>t-1, t, t+1</math> are the side lengths of a Brahmagupta triangle then, for any positive integer <math>k</math>, the integers <math>k(t-1), kt, k(t+1)</math> are the side lengths of a generalized Brahmagupta triangle which form an arithmetic progression with common difference <math>k</math>. There are generalized Brahmagupta triangles which are not generated this way. A primitive generalized Brahmagupta triangle is a generalized Brahmagupta triangle in which the side lengths have no common factor other than 1.<ref name="James">{{cite journal |last1=James A. Macdougall |title=Heron Triangles With Sides in Arithmetic Progression |journal=Journal of Recreational Mathematics |date=January 2003 |volume=31 |pages=189–196}}</ref> 

To find the side lengths of such triangles, let the side lengths be <math>t-d, t, t+d</math> where <math>t,d</math> are integers satisfying <math>1\le d\le t</math>. Using Heron's formula, the area <math>A</math> of the triangle can be shown to be 
:<math> A = \big(\tfrac{b}{4}\big)\sqrt{3(t^2-4d^2)}</math>.
For <math>A</math> to be an integer, <math>t </math> must be even and one may take <math>t=2x </math> for some integer. This makes
:<math>A=x\sqrt{3(x^2-d^2)}</math>.
Since, again, <math>A </math> has to be an integer, <math> x^2-d^2 </math> has to be in the form <math>3y^2</math> for some integer <math>y</math>. Thus, to find the side lengths of generalized Brahmagupta triangles, one has to find solutions to the following homogeneous quadratic Diophantine equation:
:<math>x^2-3y^2=d^2</math>.
It can be shown that all primitive solutions of this equation are given by<ref name=James/>
:<math>
\begin{align}
d & = \vert m^2 - 3n^2\vert /g\\
x & = (m^2 + 3n^2)/g\\
y & = 2mn/g
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>m</math> and <math>n</math> are relatively prime positive integers and <math>g = \text{gcd}(m^2 - 3n^2, 2mn, m^2 + 3n^2) </math>. 

If we take <math> m=n=1</math> we get the Brahmagupta triangle <math>(3,4,5)</math>. If we take <math> m=2, n=1</math> we get the Brahmagupta triangle <math>(13,14,15)</math>. But if we take <math> m=1, n=2</math> we get the generalized Brahmagupta triangle <math>(15, 26, 37)</math> which cannot be reduced to a Brahmagupta triangle.
